title: T1021.004 — Remote Services: SSH
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services: SSH with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: Phishing plants a keylogger
steps.caption: The attacker phishes a developer and runs a small keylogger on DEV-WS-03. SSH keys are files in the .ssh folder. Whoever reads the private key file can log in as the developer, with no password needed.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Find the way in
steps.caption: From the developer workstation, the attacker scans the production network for SSH. Port 22 answers on several servers. An internal scan is quiet, but firewall flow logs can still show it.

steps.title: Log in with the stolen key
steps.caption: The attacker logs in as the deploy user using the stolen private key. No password is needed, so no brute force is seen. The auth.log line accepts the key and even names its fingerprint.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Plant a backdoor key
steps.caption: The attacker appends a new public key to the authorized_keys file of the deploy user. From now on they can come back any time with their own key, even if the stolen one is removed.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Ride the agent to the database
steps.caption: A DBA session on PROD-APP-01 left a live agent behind, because the DBA logged in with ssh -A. The attacker points SSH at that agent socket, and the DBA's key signs the way into PROD-DB-01. The private key never leaves memory, so no file changes and no alarm fires.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Tunnel and exfiltrate
steps.caption: The attacker packs the database backups and sends them through an SSH tunnel back to the owned developer workstation. The traffic is encrypted SSH, so it looks like a normal admin transfer.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.caption: The attacker adds a small cron job on the app server and checks that the planted key is still in place. This access survives restarts, password resets, and even the removal of the first stolen key.

steps.title: How defenders catch this
steps.caption: No single line gives the attack away. The SIEM joins the story: a publickey login from a workstation subnet into production, an authorized_keys write, and one source reaching several hosts. Together they raise one high-priority case.
